14.     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY/RMP SUBMITTAL
14.1    CORPORATE PREVENTION AND EMERGENCY RESPONSE APPROACHES
At this facility, Illinois American Water Company handles chlorine for the purpose of disinfecting and treating wastewater. OSHA and EPA consider chlorine as a hazardous chemical. The hazards of chlorine make it necessary to observe certain safety precautions in the use and handling to prevent unnecessary human exposure, to reduce the threat to our own personal health as well as our co-workers, and to reduce the threat to nearby members of the community. It is Illinois American Water Company's policy to adhere to all applicable Federal and State rules and regulations. Safety depends on the manner covered process chemicals are handled and used, combined with the safety devices inherent in the design along with operating procedures and the training of our personnel.

The facility is non-responding stationary source as defined by 40CFR68.90(b), and relies on the Alton Fire Department to respond to accidental releases of chlorine and the employees of the facility will not respond. The Alton Fire Department has received a copy of the facilities Emergency Action Plan.


14.2    THE STATIONARY SOURCE AND REGULATED SUBSTANCES
The Alton Wastewater Treatment Plant is located in Madison County. The treatment process utilizes chlorine 6 months per year, from May 1st to October 31st. Chlorine is the only substance utilized in the facility's treatment process in a quantity regulated by EPA's RMP and OSHA's PSM standards.	
The maximum amount of chlorine stored at the Alton WWTP is 6,000 pounds.
The chlorine is delivered by truck in one-ton cylinders. Liquid chlorine is added to wastewater by evaporating chlorine liquid to gas, metering the gas through an injector, and then diffusing the gas into the flow stream of wastewater at the point of application.
	Senior management is committed to the safe operation of our facilities and its impact on the surrounding communities.

14.3

THE WORST-CASE RELEASE SCENARIO AND THE ALTERNATIVE RELEASE INCLUDING ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROLS AND MITIGATION MEASURES TO LIMIT THE DISTANCES FOR EACH REPORTED SCENARIO

Worst-Case Scenario:
o	Driving on the extremely rough Chessen Road causes the delivery transport vehicle's container securement device to release, unbeknownst to the driver. When making a turn with in the treatment plant property the loose container rolls off the transport trailer and drops to the ground, knocking off the valve cover and shearing a valve. This creates and uncontrolled release of 2,000 pounds of liquid and/or gaseous chlorine at a rate of 200 pounds per minute for a 10 minute duration.
o	Utilizing RMP Comp modeling for an urban setting, distance to the end point for a ground level release of chlorine (vapor density 2.49), at 77 degree F and 68% humidity, would travel 1.3 miles potentially affecting a population of 4,299 people before dispersing enough to no longer pose a significant hazard to the public.

o This scenario assumes there are no administrative controls or passive mitigation equipment, devices, or technologies that would limit the release rate or quantity.

	Alternative-Case Scenario:
o	A tubing failure at the chlorinator results in the release through a 1/16 inch diameter opening,  allowing a release rate of 0.6 pounds per minute of gaseous chlorine for a 10 minute duration for a total release of 6 pounds of chlorine.
o	Utilizing RMP Comp modeling, distance to the end point for a ground level release of chlorine at 77 degrees F and 68% humidity, would travel 0.1 miles potentially affecting a population of 0 before dispersing enough to no longer pose a significant hazard to the public. 
o This scenario assumes an indoor release whereby the building serves as passive mitigation to reduce the quantity of the release to the environment.                                                 
                                                          
14.4    THE GENERAL ACCIDENTAL RE

LEASE PREVENTION PROGRAM AND THE SPECIFIC PREVENTION STEPS
This facility and process uses design codes and standards from the Chlorine Institute, Wallace and Tiernan, American National Standards Institute, American Society for Testing and Materials, and applicable state codes and regulations.
14.5    FIVE YEAR ACCIDENT HISTORY
As of 5/19/2025, we have had no accidental releases of chlorine in the past five years.
14.6    THE EMERGENCY RESPONSE PROGRAM
The written emergency response program is located at the facility with an ongoing training program. Fire department inspections/tours are being conducted annually, detailing on-site chemicals, storage locations, chemical hazards, special instructions and requirements.
14.7    PLANNED CHANGES TO IMPROVE SAFETY
There are no immediate plans for changes to improve safety at this facility. We constantly review advancement in safety and process technology for the continuing pursuit to provide a safer workplace and community.
